# The Quartz Loop: Using Process-Part Cleaning Delays as an Early Warning of Semiconductor Supply Disruption

## Project summary

Semiconductor supply-chain research generally follows wafers, fabrication equipment, chemicals, and finished chips. This project will examine a less visible dependency: the local circulation of reusable quartz process parts between fabrication plants and specialist cleaning vendors. Quartz tubes, liners, and boats accumulate residues during deposition and diffusion processes. They are removed, transported to a cleaning facility, inspected, cleaned, and returned to the fabrication plant.

The proposal argues that delays in this loop can provide an early warning of declining semiconductor output. It will study four cleaning vendors serving the invented manufacturing region of Kestrel Bay and construct a weekly Quartz Loop Stress Index (QLSI). The index will combine turnaround time, rejected-part rates, truck delays, electricity use, and wastewater conductivity. The study will then compare the index with reported production at six fabrication plants over twelve months. Its intended result is a practical indicator that purchasing teams and regional planners can use before conventional shortage data become available.

## Background and rationale

Reusable process parts occupy an unusual position in the supply chain. They are not consumed like gases, but neither are they permanent capital equipment. A fabrication plant needs enough clean parts to replace contaminated ones without interrupting tool operation. Holding additional sets may reduce risk, yet quartz assemblies are costly, fragile, and specific to particular tools. Cleaning capacity is also geographically constrained because transport increases breakage risk and turnaround time.

Existing supply-chain dashboards tend to emphasize international trade and inventories. These measures may detect major disruptions but overlook operational congestion near fabrication sites. A cleaning vendor could therefore become a bottleneck even when global supplies of wafers and chemicals remain adequate. Preliminary conversations with two operations managers at the fictional firms ClearArc Services and LumenBath suggest that turnaround times sometimes double during periods of high demand. Because both managers described cleaning delays shortly before production problems at customer plants, the project treats quartz circulation as a likely leading indicator rather than merely a symptom of higher production.

## Research questions

1. Does a rise in quartz-part cleaning turnaround time precede a fall in weekly fabrication output?
2. Which observable cleaning-vendor measures provide the earliest indication of stress?
3. Can one regional index be used to estimate disruption risk for the wider domestic semiconductor industry?
4. Would procurement teams alter inventory decisions if they received the index four weeks in advance?

The principal hypothesis is that a ten-point increase in the QLSI will predict at least a five percent decline in fabrication output within four weeks.

## Study design

The project will recruit four of Kestrel Bay’s seven cleaning vendors. Vendors will be selected according to willingness to share records, while an effort will be made to include one small, two medium, and one large operation. Six fabrication plants using those vendors will also be invited. Together, these plants are expected to represent several process generations and approximately one quarter of regional wafer starts.

Each vendor will submit weekly figures for average door-to-door turnaround time, number of parts received, proportion failing inspection, overtime hours, electricity consumption, and wastewater conductivity. GPS loggers will be placed on two delivery vehicles per vendor to estimate transport delays. Researchers will conduct one site visit at the start of the project to confirm how each measure is recorded. Missing values will be replaced with the previous week’s figure so that the index remains continuous.

The QLSI will assign 40 percent of its weight to turnaround time, 20 percent to rejected parts, 15 percent to transport delays, 15 percent to electricity use, and 10 percent to wastewater conductivity. These weights reflect the research team’s view that time is the most direct sign of congestion. Each variable will be converted to a score from zero to 100 using the lowest and highest observations during the first eight weeks. Vendor scores will then be averaged, regardless of vendor size, to prevent a large supplier from dominating the indicator.

Participating fabrication plants will provide weekly wafer-start estimates, tool downtime, and output forecasts. Where plants decline to provide wafer starts, the study will substitute procurement managers’ ratings of production conditions on a five-point scale. These ratings and measured wafer starts will be combined into a single regional output series. The project assumes that managers familiar with operations can estimate output accurately enough for weekly comparison.

Eight procurement managers will receive a simulated QLSI alert in month nine. Four will see a warning that stress is rising, while four will see a stable index. They will be asked how many spare quartz sets they would purchase. A difference between the groups will be interpreted as evidence that the indicator changes inventory behavior.

## Analysis

The primary analysis will correlate each week’s QLSI with regional output one to six weeks later. The lead time with the strongest negative correlation will be selected as the index’s forecasting horizon. If the correlation exceeds 0.5, the project will conclude that cleaning-loop stress is an important cause of subsequent production losses. Vendor interviews will be used to explain weeks in which the statistical relationship is weak.

The project will also compare the QLSI with a simple average of vendor turnaround times. If the full index performs better in the same twelve-month period, it will be treated as validated. Results from Kestrel Bay will be scaled to the domestic industry according to the region’s estimated share of national fabrication capacity. For example, a two percent projected decline in Kestrel Bay will imply a proportionate national risk after adjusting for regional share.

Weather, electricity interruptions, and planned plant maintenance will be recorded in a research diary. They will not be included in the statistical model because the sample is unlikely to support several control variables. Instead, unusual weeks will be discussed in the final report.

## Outputs and practical value

The main output will be a spreadsheet dashboard that displays current QLSI values and four-week production risk. A short operating guide will tell procurement teams when to add spare quartz sets: no action below 40, review inventories between 40 and 60, and place additional orders above 60. These thresholds will be chosen by examining where output declines occurred during the study.

A second output will map cleaning capacity around Kestrel Bay. Regional development agencies could use the map to identify areas where an additional cleaning facility would reduce transport distance. Participating vendors will receive private summaries comparing their turnaround times with the anonymous group average.

## Confidentiality and limitations

Company records will be stored under codes, and no plant- or vendor-level figures will appear in public outputs. GPS data will be aggregated by trip and will not be used to assess individual drivers. Participants may review factual descriptions of their operations before publication, although they may not remove findings simply because they are unfavorable.

The twelve-month period may not include a severe disruption, and participating firms may differ from vendors that refuse access. The study will address this by collecting detailed operational data rather than expanding the sample. Quartz use also varies by fabrication process, but converting all measures to the common index scale should make plants sufficiently comparable.

## Schedule

Months one and two will cover recruitment, data agreements, and baseline measurement. Data collection will run from months three through fourteen. The manager alert exercise will occur in month nine. Analysis, interviews, and dashboard construction will take place in months fifteen through seventeen, followed by publication in month eighteen.
planted_strengths: The proposal identifies a genuinely overlooked semiconductor dependency: the local cleaning and recirculation of reusable quartz process parts.
It states concrete research questions, a falsifiable directional hypothesis, a timeline, and practical outputs rather than remaining purely conceptual.
It attempts to triangulate operational records, logistics data, interviews, and a behavioral exercise, while including reasonable confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information.
planted_weaknesses: The causal claim is unsupported: a correlation between cleaning congestion and later output would not establish that cleaning delays caused the decline, especially because high production demand, maintenance, power events, or other common factors could affect both.

The sample is a small willingness-based selection from one invented region, yet the proposal plans to extrapolate proportionally to an entire domestic industry without accounting for differences in process mix, vendor structure, geography, or quartz dependence.

The QLSI weights and thresholds are arbitrary, its normalization relies on only eight baseline weeks, equal vendor weighting discards exposure differences, and carrying the previous observation forward can conceal disruptions.
The outcome measure improperly combines actual wafer starts with subjective five-point manager ratings, producing a regional series whose units and comparability are undefined.

The analysis selects whichever forecast horizon has the strongest correlation and validates the index on the same twelve-month dataset, creating substantial overfitting and multiple-testing problems without an out-of-sample test or uncertainty estimates. The proposed sample of eight managers is also too small to support the claimed behavioral inference.
quality_rationale: The proposal earns credit for an original and operationally relevant angle, clear organization, specific data sources, and attention to commercial confidentiality. However, its central inference is methodologically weak. It uses a small convenience sample, combines incompatible outcomes, invents index weights without calibration, selects the best-performing lag after observing the data, and treats correlation as causation. Its national extrapolation and eight-person behavioral exercise are particularly unjustified. These are fundamental design problems that prevent the proposed study from reliably answering its research questions, despite several promising conceptual features.
title: The Quartz Loop: Using Process-Part Cleaning Delays as an Early Warning of Semiconductor Supply Disruption
topic: Whether congestion among specialist quartz process-part cleaning vendors can serve as an early warning of semiconductor fabrication slowdowns.
